name: Hypertensive emergency

matching.reasoningTemplate: Severe hypertension with headache, visual or neurological symptoms indicates a hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage.

redFlags: Controlled BP reduction; identify target-organ damage

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e p.2148 (hypertensive urgencies & emergencies), p.2153-2154 (malignant hypertension / arteriolonephrosclerosis), p.190-192 (coma evaluation, PRES/hyperperfusion syndromes), p.227 (hypertensive retinopathy), p.2871 (scleroderma renal crisis)
clinicalPearls: The threshold prompting concern for a crisis is typically a markedly elevated BP, often described as SBP/DBP at or above ~180/100-120 mmHg; however the level alone does not define an emergency — the presence of acute, ongoing end-organ injury does (p.2148).

Urgency vs emergency is a functional distinction: an asymptomatic patient without evidence of active end-organ damage has an urgency (manageable with oral agents in the outpatient setting), whereas demonstrable acute target-organ injury makes it an emergency requiring IV therapy with close inpatient/ER supervision (p.2148).
Hypertensive urgency is far more common than true emergency; over-treating urgency as if it were an emergency risks harm from excessive BP lowering (p.2148).

Certain syndromes — acute aortic dissection, eclampsia or severe pre-eclampsia, and pheochromocytoma in crisis — flag a need for particularly rapid, aggressive BP control compared with other emergencies (p.2148).

After the acute BP is brought under control, look for secondary causes of hypertension — renovascular disease in particular is relatively common among patients presenting with a hypertensive emergency (p.2148).
Malignant hypertension most often arises in a patient with known, treated hypertension who has stopped taking medications, or who uses vasospastic drugs such as cocaine (p.2153-2154).
In acute hypertensive retinopathy, BP must not be lowered precipitously: an abrupt drop risks optic disc infarction and worsening visual loss (p.227).
harrison.pathophysiology: Severe, rapidly progressive BP elevation produces mechanical/pressure-related vascular injury that overwhelms protective vascular tone. In malignant hypertension the characteristic lesion is fibrinoid necrosis of small vessels — breakdown of the vessel wall with deposition of eosinophilic fibrin-containing material and a perivascular cellular infiltrate; larger interlobular arteries may show a hyperplastic 'onionskin' proliferative lesion. These changes can obliterate glomeruli and tubular structures, driving progressive kidney failure. Multiple pathways can generate this pressure injury, including activation of the renin-angiotensin system and intense vasospasm from catecholamine release; when endothelial injury is severe enough it triggers microangiopathic hemolysis. Cerebral involvement reflects failure of cerebral blood-flow autoregulation: at extreme pressures autoregulatory limits are exceeded, producing hyperperfusion, vasogenic edema and the encephalopathy/PRES picture — which is also why too-rapid lowering below the autoregulatory range can cause cerebral or optic ischemia (p.2153-2154, p.192, p.227).
additionalDifferentials: Scleroderma renal crisis — accelerated hypertension with AKI, clinically indistinguishable from malignant hypertension; consider in systemic sclerosis, especially diffuse/progressive skin disease, anti-RNA-polymerase-III antibody, or recent glucocorticoid exposure (p.2871).
Pheochromocytoma in crisis — catecholamine surge causing paroxysmal severe hypertension (p.2148).
Eclampsia / severe pre-eclampsia in a pregnant or peripartum patient (p.2148).
nonInfectiousMimics: Cocaine or other vasospastic-drug-induced severe hypertension (can precipitate malignant-phase hypertension) (p.2153-2154).
Thrombotic microangiopathies (TTP/HUS) which overlap with the microangiopathic hemolysis seen in malignant hypertension (p.2153-2154).
additionalInvestigations: Funduscopy for hypertensive end-organ change — arteriolar sclerosis/narrowing, splinter (flame) hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots (nerve-fiber-layer infarcts), hard exudates into the macula, and papilledema (p.227, p.190).
CBC with peripheral smear and reticulocytes to detect microangiopathic hemolysis — anemia, schistocytes, reticulocytosis (p.2153-2154).
Urinalysis — hematuria, proteinuria, granular/nephritic sediment in renal involvement (p.2153-2154, p.2871).
Serum creatinine to detect/track acute kidney injury (p.2153-2154).
Once BP is controlled, work-up for secondary hypertension, especially renovascular imaging (p.2148).
redFlags: Hypertensive encephalopathy — headache, visual disturbance, nausea/vomiting, seizures, altered consciousness (p.2148).
Acute left ventricular failure / pulmonary edema in the setting of severe hypertension (p.2148).
Acute kidney failure with severe hypertension (p.2148).
Papilledema, retinal hemorrhages or acute visual loss (signs of malignant-phase / hypertensive retinopathy) (p.2153-2154, p.227).
Features suggesting a rapid-care syndrome: chest/back pain (aortic dissection), pregnancy with seizures (eclampsia), or paroxysmal catecholamine symptoms (pheochromocytoma) (p.2148).
harrison.prognosis: Untreated malignant-phase hypertension with target-organ injury (papilledema, declining kidney function) historically carried mortality exceeding 50% over 6-12 months, with older reports of >90% one-year mortality before effective drug therapy — hence the term 'malignant'. With effective BP reduction, manifestations of vascular injury including microangiopathic hemolysis and renal dysfunction can improve over time, and current 5-year survival exceeds 50% (p.2153-2154).
pitfalls: Treating an asymptomatic high BP (urgency) with aggressive IV agents as though it were an emergency, risking harm from over-rapid lowering (p.2148).

Aiming for immediate normalization of BP — a controlled reduction rather than normalization is sufficient, followed by transition to oral agents; potent IV vasodilators can overshoot and cause hypotension (p.2148).
Lowering BP precipitously in acute hypertensive retinopathy or cerebral involvement, where falling below the autoregulatory range risks optic disc or cerebral infarction (p.227).
Missing a treatable secondary cause (notably renovascular disease) by not investigating after acute control (p.2148).
Overlooking normotensive scleroderma renal crisis — ~10% present with BP in the normal range and carry a poor outcome (p.2871).
harrison.severityClassification: Hypertensive urgency = markedly elevated BP (e.g., SBP/DBP >=180/100 mmHg) in an asymptomatic patient WITHOUT evidence of acute ongoing end-organ damage — manage with oral agents as outpatient. Hypertensive emergency = comparably high BP WITH evidence of active end-organ injury (encephalopathy, acute LV failure/pulmonary edema, acute kidney failure, retinal hemorrhage/papilledema, dissection, eclampsia, pheochromocytoma crisis) — requires immediate, carefully supervised IV therapy in ER/inpatient setting. Malignant hypertension is the severe phenotype defined by rapidly progressive BP elevation with fibrinoid-necrosis vascular injury, retinal hemorrhages/papilledema, encephalopathy and declining kidney function (p.2148, p.2153-2154).
